chapter_theme: Natrinai 241 to 260: the seasons and the night in the voices of the friend and the wife; the friend reads omens and denies the rains, presses the hill lord to marry because the millet is ripening and the girl is shut in, and plays the shore lord's suit, while the wife grieves wealth set above virtue, shies from her husband at their son's side, and men give up or hurry back from journeys with the stag and his doe as their emblem.

241.reading: The woman asks her friend whether they do not think of her, the men who left her for the restless sickness of wealth, now that the water has drawn back to show wet fine sand printed with the feet of curve-winged birds, the northern wind stirs the reed's white flowers till they deck the bush like the whisk a king waves, and the sun, in a sky cleared of rain, opens and shuts like a blinking eye and is gone, so that in the dewy midnight her kohl-lined eyes run with tears.
241.nuance: Everything she names is a sign of the cold season settling in: the receded water, the north wind, the reed in flower, a sun that only blinks between clouds. The question is not whether he remembers her in general but whether this season, which she reads hour by hour from dusk to midnight, reaches him where he is.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone for wealth and she grieves the parting; the things around her are of the river bank

comparisons.tenor: the reed's white flowers spread over the bush
the sun showing and hiding between clouds

242.reading: Returning with his work done, the man sees the rains begin (the leafless pidavam budding, the thalavam vine opening on the bush, konrai flowering like gold and kaayaa crowding its twigs with gem-blue blossom) and tells his charioteer to drive fast this morning, pointing to the stag on the salt flat who, when the herd fled with his young doe, stands with a longing heart, not leaving, searching for her.
242.nuance: The poet's name, Vizhikkat Pethai Perungannanar, is taken from line 8, the wide-eyed doe. The stag is the one creature in the poem that does not move: everything else opens, blooms or flees, and he stands searching, which is the man's state put outside him.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மறுத்தராநின்ற தலைமகன் கார் கண்டு பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the flowers of the first rains and the returning man fix mullai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாக, line 6)

iraicchi.act: when the herd scatters, the stag does not run with it but stands searching for his young doe
iraicchi.sense: the man too will not rest until he has found his wife again, so the chariot must hurry

243.reading: The woman says that the dark koel, staying in every grove of the fragrant mango on the bank of the clear stream below the honeyed slope, sits body to body with its mate and calls lovingly, as if rebuking those who leave helplessly, 'wise ones, do not go away and leave a life that does not stay, like dice turned over'; and if parting for wealth even in such a painful season is the nature of men, then wealth, surely, is dearer than virtue.
243.nuance: The last line turns the moral order upside down on purpose: by men's conduct wealth is rated above virtue. The koel's call is given words by the speaker herself, so the rebuke she cannot speak to him she puts in a bird's mouth.

thinai_evidence.note: a parting for wealth; the hill stream and mango grove are not its own land

comparisons.tenor: a life that does not stay

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the poem speaks of men in general

244.reading: The girl tells her friend she is cruel: she could tell the lord of the high hill, where on the cool rain-soaked slope the koothalam flower of the cold season smells and the asunam listens to the sweet humming of bees, or she could tell the mother, who does not know where the grief comes from, that this is how the sickness will abate; she does neither, though she has seen the pallor on the girl's body, like the tender shoots of the asoka on the tall gem-bright hill.
244.nuance: She sets out the friend's two possible acts as a choice (ஒன்றோ ... ஒன்றோ) and blames her for taking neither, which is the moment of அறத்தொடுநிலை from the girl's side. The asunam, an animal that hangs on music, listening to bees, is scene; read as a hint that the girl too is held by sweet sound it is a single match of mood, not iraicchi.

colophon.thurai: அறத்தொடுநிலை வலித்த தோழியைத் தலைவி முகம் புக்கது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope, its creature and its trees, and a secret love not yet told

245.reading: The friend, who has agreed to help him, tells the girl it makes her laugh: when they had woven a garland of mundakam flowers into her gem-dark hair and played with their companions in the clear sea, the shore lord reined in the horses of his tall chariot and, asking 'who are you, slender-waisted, sweet-spoken, who have seized my life?', told them how he had been struck, never knowing that he was striking them, and stood with joined hands gazing at her bright brow.
245.nuance: The joke is the reversal: the man reports himself as the victim of an அணங்கு, while the girls are the ones afflicted, so each side thinks itself the one struck. The friend makes the girl laugh in order to open her to the man's suit.

colophon.thurai: குறை நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளை முகம் புக்கது

thinai_evidence.note: the sea, the shore grove and its water-thorn flowers

246.reading: The friend tells the wasting woman that he will come and does not lie, though he crossed many wastes with a firm heart for wealth to be made: the lizard on the long wall chirps sweetly on the lucky side, the dark koel on the top branch of the house's nochchi calls again and again, and in the scrub the golden konrai is out with the pidavu buds opening and the sky rumbling with sweet sound; is this not the season he named when he said 'we will come'?
246.nuance: The reassurance moves from the house outward: two household omens first (the lizard, the koel on the nochchi by the door), then the land, then the sky, and it closes as a question, so the friend's certainty is offered for the woman to confirm. The colophon's thinai is paalai, by the man's road; what the poem shows is the waiting at home in the rains.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the waiting for a promised return in the rains; the waste is only where he went

247.reading: The friend tells the hill lord, in whose land the sweet-voiced cloud, having poured heavy drops that wash the red tusks of an elephant killed in a fierce old enmity, turns to carded cotton and plays over the tall peaks at dawn, that even if he does not grant grace, even if he does unkind things, her fair-browed friend will follow his way; and that he knows well there is no medicine but him for the pallor that has come to her like a guest.
247.nuance: The pallor is a விருந்து, a guest who has settled in the house; a guest is fed and kept, so the figure says the girl's sickness is now at home with her. The killed elephant whose tusks the rain washes is scene; a reading of it as the danger he runs, or as a wrong the rain cleans away, has only one point of contact.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, its elephant and its morning cloud, and a lover pressed to marry

comparisons.tenor: the pallor that has settled on her

248.reading: Addressing the cloud, the friend says that he said the season would be when the small honey-scented mullai flowers bloom to adorn the cool bush like the spotted face of the striped deer and the rich rain comes; now, lacking love, the cloud practises unkindness with the roaring voice of false thunder to see the suffering heart tremble; but will she be fooled like the flock of young peacocks that take it for true and dance? Long live, cloud!
248.nuance: She grants that the signs look right and refuses them: the thunder is பொய், and she sets herself apart from the peafowl who believe it. To deny the season is to keep the man's promise unbroken, since if this is not the season he is not late.

colophon.thurai: பருவம் கண்டு ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகளைத் தோழி மழை மேல் வைத்துப் பருவம் மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai in flower and the season of rain awaited

comparisons.vehicle: பொறி வரி நல் மான் புகர் முகம் கடுப்ப
comparisons.tenor: the mullai flowers spread over the bush
herself, if she believed the thunder

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: spoken to the cloud (மழையே, line 9) for the woman to hear

249.reading: The shore lord's chariot came clattering into the rich street and went, setting gossip rising in the old whispering town: there, under the punnai with its trunk like iron, leaves like sapphire, clusters like silver and pollen like gold falling between, the striped bees hummed on the horse's flower-scented neck, spotted like a tiger with the pollen, and the horse, taking itself for set upon by a tiger, leapt like a ball and would not stand however it was reined.
249.nuance: The chain of causes is comic and exact: pollen spots the horse, bees come to the pollen, the horse takes the spots and the humming for a tiger, bolts, and the noise in the street announces what the lovers kept secret. The poem ends on the chariot going, so the gossip outlasts the visit.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai of the shore and the shore lord

comparisons.tenor: the pollen-spotted neck of the horse

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names neither speaker nor addressee; the girl wasting before the marriage is the likeliest speaker

250.reading: The man, come home with his son, tells the bard to come and laugh with him: when his sweet-lisping son, anklets ringing, was practising walking his little chariot in the street, his flower-scented red mouth smeared with sandal paste, the man, his heart urging him, came close wanting to hug him, and his beloved, with her crescent-lovely brow and fragrant dark hair, taking it otherwise, shied away like a startled doe and stood apart, saying 'who are you?'
250.nuance: The joke is against himself: the wife greets her own husband with the question a stranger gets. He used the son as his way back into the house, and she reads even his embrace of the child as coming from elsewhere; the 'laugh' covers his failure.

colophon.thurai: புதல்வனொடு புக்க தலைமகன் ஆற்றானாய்ப் பாணற்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's estranged sulking at the husband returning by way of the son

251.reading: With the man listening outside, the speaker turns to the millet: in the land of the good hill where the falls roar and a female monkey snatches the fine fruit from the thick stem of the great wild plantain, we, loving its lord, have guarded you with great love and driven the birds off your ears, you have seen it; now that the old beauty of my shoot-like body is fading and the household, worshipping the god of offerings, makes a festival, do not bend your ears for the swaying birds to snatch, but rise and ripen late, long live, millet!
251.nuance: The plea to the millet is the news the man is meant to hear: when the crop is in, the girl's days in the field end and she is shut in the house. Whether the festival for the god is a harvest rite or the mother's remedy for the girl's changed looks, the text does not settle.

thinai_evidence.note: falls, monkey and millet of the hill, and a secret love at risk

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: spoken to the millet (தினையே, line 11); the colophon names no speaker, and the 'my body' of line 7 may make it the girl

iraicchi.act: the female monkey takes the ripe fruit from the plant while it is there to be taken
iraicchi.sense: the man should take the girl now, while she is still in the field, before the harvest shuts her away

252.reading: The friend tells the anxious woman that his heart, once unresolved, resolved on the far country's track where the dead oomai stands bent and cicadas shrill, holding that rare wealth does not gather for those who stay unless they go with a firm will and act; but the work so planned seems to be blocked by her qualities: her blameless look like a doll on a painted wall, her wide hips, her dark rain-eyes like flowers strung in pairs, her small feet like the good tongue of the fierce dog leaping to hunt a hare, and her full hair and fine jewels.
252.nuance: The man's maxim is given its full weight before it is checked, and what checks it is not counter-argument but a list of her features: the friend comforts her by telling her what her own beauty does to his resolve. The dog's tongue simile, red and soft and narrow, is the oddest and most exact of the set.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரியும் எனக் கவன்ற தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the dry waste of withered trees and cicadas, and a planned going for wealth

comparisons.vehicle: முடுகு விசைக் கத நாய் நல் நாப் புரையும்

253.reading: The friend tells the man that when birds return to their roosts or he sees couples together he sighs hot breaths like a stalled elephant, wasting with pain, and does not hear her, only thinks; the bright-jewelled girl, whom one trembles even to think of, has come to great beauty and is now hard to reach, guarded like the jackfruit-laden hill of Paari, generous with many pots of toddy, where thunder of great sound and rain have closed round.
253.nuance: Paari's hill is the measure of both beauty and inaccessibility: rich and besieged, it could not be taken by force. The friend's point is that the time for stealing visits is over.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl now guarded and a lover pressed to marry, with a hill for the image

comparisons.tenor: the girl, grown beautiful and closely guarded

254.reading: The friend tells the lord of the wide roaring sea, who built sand houses with them, kicked the incoming waves, plucked the adumbu creeper on the high white dune and spoke sweet words without sulking, but got no answer and is going away slowly, wearied, that if he stays in their small hamlet by the shore, whose farming (changing the water with small straight staves) needs no rain, and eats today the rice bartered for the salt the umanar brought, he will not sleep alone with no companion, his chest where the large blue-lily garland rolls.
254.nuance: The colophon says the friend says what she has made up (படைத்து மொழிந்தது): the invitation is a test or a feint, and the reader cannot tell whether the companion she promises is the girl. The salt pan, farming that needs no sky, is a picture of the shore people's self-sufficiency set against the man's need.

thinai_evidence.note: the dune creeper, the salt traders and the shore hamlet

255.reading: The girl says the ghouls stir and the town has gone to sleep, the hill folk of the guarded house stay awake singing the awesome kurinji, and the sword-striped tiger that fought a strong tusker roars on the slope of rock caves; alas, though our soft shoulders loosen and we suffer, it would be good if he did not come tonight, by the path on the high hill where lightning flashes on the ridges, rain and wind mingle past midnight, the snake wanders searching for its gem and the thunder, red, strikes.
255.nuance: She wishes away the meeting she longs for, setting her own wasting (மென் தோள் நெகிழ்ந்து) against his danger and choosing his safety; the path itself is the poem's subject, as the colophon's ஆறு பார்த்து says.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight on the hill, the hill folk's song, the tiger and the night tryst

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the girl speaks of 'our' shoulders and 'him'

256.reading: The man tells his wife, who grieved thinking he had left for wealth: you have small blameless feet worth singing, great beauty and warring eyes, while the forest's trees, seized by fire, have lost the beauty of their shade, and loneliness sits enthroned there; so we have given up going; and even the cool forest of the rains, when the kalaa blooms with the pidavu and the dark-necked stag, holding his young doe, rests in the striped shade of the thorny vela tree, we have given that up too.
256.nuance: He renounces both seasons of the road, the burnt summer forest and the pleasant forest of the rains, and the doubled refrain (தவிர்ந்தனம் செலவே) is the promise. The stag who holds his doe in the shade is what he chooses to be.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்தான் என்று ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைமகளைத் தலைமகன் ஆற்றியது

thinai_evidence.note: a journey given up; the scorched forest is paalai's and the rain forest mullai's

iraicchi.act: the stag holds his young doe close and rests with her in the shade
iraicchi.sense: the man will stay and keep his wife as the stag keeps his doe, even in the season that invites travel

257.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, where cloud has risen with endless roar and pouring drops and settled on the cold dripping slope, bamboo grows thick to the sky on the tall peak, white falls shine on the side of the wide hill and the dark-trunked vengai's gold-like fragrant flowers spread on the rock, that he loves but is not gracious: knowing that fierce beasts roam the narrow path by the pools where no traveller goes, he comes at midnight, and she grieves for it.
257.nuance: 'You love, yet you are not gracious' splits the man's two duties: desire brings him at midnight, but grace would spare her the fear, which only marriage can do. The scene is all beauty; the danger is stated in two lines without description.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகனது ஏதம் சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope, the vengai and the midnight visit

258.reading: The friend tells the shore lord that she is going, she who frequented the day trysts in the flowered shore grove: the mother has shut the girl in, seeing her close-fitting bright bangles slipping, the girl who is like the port of Marungur, where the gold-bangled women of the rich wide houses spill at the back door the rice, like heron's claws, cooked for arriving guests, and the fresh-eyed crow, having eaten it while the sun burns the rocks, at dusk snatches the fresh prawns heaped in the shade of the market and roosts on the mast of a rocking ship.
258.nuance: The comparison runs on the port's fullness, a whole day of plenty from the guest's rice to the roost on the mast, and the girl is like that abundance; the crow that eats freely all day is set against the girl now shut in. Read as the man feeding at will, the crow has one point of contact, not two, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove, the prawns, the ships and the port

259.reading: The friend asks the girl what they will do: the friendship they made in great delight with the lord of the great-rock land, on the honey-scented slope where the gold-flowered vengai stands tall (staying in the wide millet field, chasing the red-beaked green parrots, bathing in the falls of the great hill's side, smoothing on the slope's sandal where bees settle), she now sees becoming very hard to keep, for the millet heads have taken their dry ripeness, like the spreading waves of the sea drawing back.
259.nuance: The list of shared pleasures is all of the field season, so the ripened millet ends the whole catalogue at once; the sea simile in a hill poem measures the field's change from green waves to dry stalks.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளைச் செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇ வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, parrots, millet and the hill lord's friendship

260.reading: The wife tells the lord of the town, where the dark-legged buffalo, having grazed on the red lilies and tired of the cold lotus of the field, walks like warriors with staves and sleeps on the hill-high white sand nearby, that he embraces her as if he desired her; but he who withered the bud-opened garland once adorned to beautify her thick hair, beautiful as Iruppai at the flood-fed gate of the red-speared warrior who wore down his foes, was her enemy, and she cannot forget it and be at peace.
260.nuance: 'My enemy' (பகைவன்மன்) is said with the regretful மன்: he was, once, the man who spoiled her garland in love; now he is the man who spoils it by neglect, and the old embrace makes the new one a counterfeit.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulking at a straying husband, in the field country of the buffalo

comparisons.tenor: the husband who goes from woman to woman

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the women he goes to

pairs.situation: he has had his fill of one woman

pairs.scene: அயலது குன்று சேர் வெண் மணல் துஞ்சும்
pairs.situation: he sleeps away from home, not in his wife's house

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the buffalo of her own field town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

links.note: Both open with the same words, உள்ளார் கொல்லோ தோழி: in Kuruntokai 16 the woman pictures the kalli waste he crossed, a lizard calling its mate with a sound like thieves testing arrows; in Natrinai 241 she pictures her own surroundings, the reed flowering in the north wind and the dewy midnight.
links.teaches: Read together, the formula question can be answered from either end of the separation, the dangers of his road or the season at her door, so 'do they not think of us' is a frame into which the poet sets whichever world the woman imagines, and the choice of world is the poem's real statement.

links.note: Kural 754 says wealth rightly gained yields virtue and pleasure, placing wealth below and in service of aram; Natrinai 243's woman says that if parting for wealth in such a season is men's nature, wealth must be dearer than aram itself. On the plain reading men's conduct, as she sees it, contradicts the Kural's ordering.
links.teaches: The pair shows the Kural's ordering of virtue over wealth being turned into an accusation from inside the household: the woman accepts the scale but finds that men's going inverts it, so the ethical rule became a weapon in the akam speaker's mouth.

links.note: The same question, யாரையோ, is asked in both: in 245 the shore lord, struck at first sight, asks the girl 'who are you?'; in 250 the wife, estranged, asks her husband 'who are you?' as he comes to embrace their son.
links.teaches: Holding the two together traces the question across the whole course of akam love, from the wonder of a stranger at first meeting to a wife's pretended non-recognition in sulking, so the same words that began the bond are later used to deny it.

links.note: In Natrinai 246 the friend reassures the woman with a lizard chirping on the lucky side, a koel on the house's nochchi and the season's flowers; in Kar Narpathu 12 she calls his coming certain because the dark clouds rise every day on the right.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the friend's reassurance in the rains rested on reading omens, the right side being lucky in both, and that the rainy season itself was read as one more omen of return, which is why Natrinai 246 can end its certainty as a question.

links.note: Kural 1102 has the man say that this jewelled girl is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes; Natrinai 247's friend tells the man that for the girl's pallor there is no medicine other than him.
links.teaches: Read together, the cure that is also the cause belongs to both lovers, and the Natrinai shows the claim used as pressure: what the man says of her in delight, the friend turns back on him as an argument that only marriage can treat the girl's sickness.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 66 the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking untimely rain for the season the man named; in Natrinai 248 she calls the thunder false and refuses to be fooled like the young peafowl who dance at it.
links.teaches: The pair shows a fixed move of the friend's, denying the season by calling some creature of the land deceived, and in Natrinai 248 the move turns inward, since she speaks of herself as the one who will not be fooled, so the device is an argument about belief, not about weather.

links.note: In Kar Narpathu 1 the friend says that with the sky roaring and pouring, the man who said 'we will come' can hardly fail to come now; in Natrinai 248 the friend says the same roar is false thunder and not the promised season. On the plain reading the two friends make incompatible claims about what the rain shows.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the same evidence serves the friend either way: when the season must mean his return she affirms it, and when his absence would make him a liar she denies it, so the season's sign was something the friend argued about rather than read off.

links.note: In Akananuru 16 the wife finds a courtesan secretly embracing her son in the chariot street; in Natrinai 250 the husband goes to embrace the son in the street and the wife, taking it otherwise, shies away.
links.teaches: Read together, the small son in the street is where the marriage's suspicions are read from both sides, another woman betraying herself by loving him and the husband being refused because of what his embrace carries, so the child who should join the parents becomes the evidence between them.

links.note: Kural 616 says effort brings prosperity and its absence brings want; Natrinai 252 states the same as the man's resolve (no rare wealth for those who stay) and then shows the planned work blocked by the woman's beauty.
links.teaches: The pair shows the maxim of effort accepted in full by the lover and yet not acted on, so the Natrinai marks the limit of the Kural's rule: it decides nothing while something dearer than prosperity stands in the way.

links.note: Both are by Kapilar: in Purananuru 109 the kings besieging Paari's Parambu, with its jackfruit and its springs, cannot take it by force, but bards who come singing will be given it; in Natrinai 253 the girl, grown beautiful and hard to reach, is like Paari's jackfruit hill closed in by rain.
links.teaches: Read with the puram poem, the akam simile carries its argument: Parambu yields not to siege but to those who come asking, so the friend's comparison tells the man that the girl will not be had by stealth but only by asking for her in marriage.

links.note: In Purananuru 337 a girl courted by kings is hard to see, like the cold spring of Paari's Parambu, shut in the house while her brothers fight the suitors; in Natrinai 253 the girl, guarded like Paari's hill, is hard to reach for her secret lover.
links.teaches: The pair shows Parambu as the standard image of the guarded marriageable girl in both akam and puram, and sets two kinds of suitor against the same closed house: kings who would take her by war and a lover who must now stop coming by night.

links.note: Both are the girl's fear for the man on the hill path at midnight in rain: Akananuru 72 lists the path's dangers (a tiger that killed an elephant, a snake's gem, crocodiles) and ends by blaming herself; Natrinai 255 lists ghouls, a tiger that fought a tusker, the snake searching for its gem and thunder, and ends by wishing he would not come.
links.teaches: Read together, the same catalogue of night dangers leads to two different conclusions, self-blame for drawing him out and the wish that he stay away, so the poets used the fixed list as a premise and placed the girl's character in what she concludes from it.

links.note: Kuruntokai 375 says it is good if he does not come today because the millet has ripened and the night watchmen beat their drum at midnight; Natrinai 255 says the same, வாரார்ஆயினோ நன்றுமன், because of ghouls, a tiger, a snake and thunder on his path.
links.teaches: The two give the same wish two different reasons, discovery by the watchmen and death on the path, so the wish that he not come is a set response whose grounds range from the secret to his life, and Natrinai 255 shows the graver one.

links.note: Kural 1151 says: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 256 is the man telling his grieving wife that he has given up going, through the burnt forest and even through the cool forest of the rains.
links.teaches: Read together, the Natrinai supplies the one answer the Kural's speaker would accept, a plain 'I am not going', and shows that to be believed it had to renounce the pleasant season as well as the harsh one, since a man who stays only while the road is burnt will go when it rains.

links.note: In both the stag (இரலை) with his young doe is shown to the reader in the rains: in 242 he stands searching for her when the herd scatters, and the returning man hurries; in 256 he rests holding her in the shade, and the man gives up going.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows the iraicchi's sense fixed while the man's act changes: the stag keeping to his doe stands for the man's duty to his wife both when he hurries home and when he declines to leave.

links.note: In 255 the girl fears the midnight path for him and wishes he would not come; in 257 the friend tells the man himself that she knows fierce beasts roam the path and he still comes at midnight, and presses marriage.
links.teaches: The pair shows one danger serving two speakers: the girl's private fear in 255 becomes in the friend's mouth in 257 a lever on the man, so the convention of the dangerous path is both a feeling and an argument for marriage.

links.note: In 251 the speaker begs the millet to ripen late so the girl's days in the field may last; in 259 the millet heads have ripened like the sea drawing back, and the friend asks what they will do.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the two poems are the before and after of one threat, making the millet's ripening the clock of the secret love: the harvest that ends the field season also ends the meetings unless the man marries.

links.note: Both use the marutham buffalo as ullurai for the straying husband: in Akananuru 46 it breaks its tether at night, scatters the fish and grazes the lotus; in Natrinai 260 it has grazed the red lilies, tired of the lotus, and sleeps on the sand away from the field.
links.teaches: Read together, the one creature carries different stages of the husband's straying, the breaking out in Akananuru 46 and the surfeit and sleeping elsewhere in Natrinai 260, so the buffalo ullurai was a fixed vehicle whose actions the poets chose to fit the moment of the quarrel.

source_issues: Natrinai colophons give speaker, addressee and occasion in prose; where they name no speaker or addressee (243, 249, 251, 255) the code is my inference or pira, with a note.
246: the colophon thinai is பாலை; the poem is the waiting at home in the rains (konrai, pidavu, thunder), so I infer mullai.
251: the colophon names no speaker; 'my body' (line 7) could make the girl the speaker rather than the friend; the sense of நயவா (line 4) is unsure.
254: the sense of lines 10 and 11 (the salt pans' staves) and of who the promised companion is cannot be fixed.
253: the colophon's அறிவிறீஇ is apparently a misprint for அறிவுறீஇ (as in 251, 258, 259).
